subtopic: MR. GORDON-STATEMENT RESPECTING ACQUISITION OF MERCANTILE BANK SHARES
MR. GORDON-STATEMENT RESPECTING ACQUISITION OF MERCANTILE BANK SHARES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege in connection with a statement released yesterday afternoon by Mr. Robert P. McFadden, president of the Mercantile Bank of Canada, following a meeting of the directors of the bank. The statement begins as follows:
We believe it improper to engage in debate with the former finance minister over who said what at a meeting over three years ago. Suffice it to say we voluntarily made the full details of the transaction known to Mr. Gordon at the time and our understanding of what transpired at the meeting with him is not in accord with his.
The transaction raferred to was the acquisition of the shares of the Mercantile Bank of Canada by the First National City Bank of New York. The comment refers to what Mr. James Stillman Rockefeller, at the time president and now chairman of the First National City Bank, and Mr. McFadden, then an officer of that bank, told me at a meeting in my office on July 18, 1963, when I was minister of finance.
Mr. R. B. Bryce, deputy minister of finance, and Mr. Clayton Elderkin, inspector general of banks, were present with me during the meeting and Mr. Elderkin prepared a full report on what took place immediately afterward. The report was reviewed and concurred in by Mr. Bryce. This report leaves no doubt whatever as to what transpired despite Mr. McFadden's protestations to the contrary. I expect both Mr. Bryce and Mr. Elderkin will be called upon to confirm it when the Bank Act is up for revision.
While the statement that Mr. McFadden released yesterday is carefully worded and may sound plausible on a cursory reading, the fact of the matter is that he is questioning the accuracy of what I said in the house on June 14, 1965 in the course of my duties as minister of finance, which may be found at pages 2371 to 2373 of Hansard, and which I referred to on pages 94 and 95 of my recent book.
In my statement to the house, which was a long one, I referred to my conversation with Mr. Rockefeller and Mr. McFadden in some detail. It is on the record and I shall not repeat it except to say that I assumed the purpose of Mr. Rockefeller's visit was to ascertain, before any commitment was undertaken, whether the Canadian government of the day would be favourable to his bank acquiring control of the Mercantile Bank.
I informed Mr. Rockefeller that this would not be looked upon with favour by the Canadian government for the reasons which are set out in Hansard.
Mr. McFadden, the president of the Mercantile Bank, has now seen fit to question the accuracy of the statement which I made to the house on June 14, 1965. In doing so he has cast a reflection upon my integrity both as a member of this house and as a former member of the government.
I can only presume that this had been done deliberately. If it were to go unchallenged it might not only reflect on my veracity and therefore on my personal integrity, but it might mislead members of the house and members of the public at a time when decisions respecting the future position of the Mercantile Bank of Canada will be under

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON PATENT LICENSING OF DRUG MANUFACTURERS

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON PATENT LICENSING OF DRUG MANUFACTURERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with leave of the house I should like to table copies, in English and in French, of the report of the special committee which was established to look into matters involved in the patent licensing of drug manufacturers. This committee, which was established on June 14, 1965, consisted of Dr. Irwin Hilliard, Dr. Charles Gowdey and Dr. Roger Gaudry.
In general the various recommendations of the committee which are not directly within existing regulations are being considered, and to the extent necessary are being implemented by appropriate arrangements with the commissioner of patents, as well as by changes in our drug regulations.
Arrangements have been discussed with the commissioner of patents to ensure close cooperation between the food and drug directorate and his office. The directorate will provide the necessary report to the commissioner relating to the competency of the applicant to manufacture a particular drug,


and while the decision with respect to the issuance of a compulsory licence is entirely within the discretion of the commissioner, I consider that the arrangements which have been discussed will effectively take into account the views of the committee.
The recommendation of the committee with respect to the furnishing of samples and informational material to the food and drug directorate and the inspection of premises, are matters which can be taken care of under the authority of our existing regulations. Hon. members can be assured that careful attention will be given to the supervision of matters which are involved in this portion of the recommendations.
We have also under consideration an amendment to the definition of a new drug, which is designed to give effect to the purpose of the fifth recommendation which is contained in the report. It is felt that the existing regulations which require suitable conditions of manufacture for a drug are sufficiently broad to cover the purposes of recommendation No. 6.
The question of adequate direction for use, including information to the professions, is a matter that has been under consideration for some time and appropriate steps are being taken to amend the regulations as would be necessary to give effect to this part of the report.
As regards notification, I expect that the necessary regulations in this regard will be in force within a very short space of time. Consideration is being given to strengthening the regulations with respect to the testing of drugs imported into Canada. The present regulations require that the container of a drug in dosage form bear a lot number. My officers are looking into the practicability of the individual capsule or tablet carrying a distinctive mark.
In concluding my remarks I would like on behalf of my colleague the Secretary of State, who established the committee, and myself, to pay particular tribute to it for its willingness to undertake this work at short notice and for the quality of the report which it provided.

This is the second of three measures which are necessitated by the movement toward collective bargaining in the civil service of Canada. Under this particular measure the Civil Service Act is to be replaced by a new statute to be known as the public service employment act. This measure will not only retain the merit system of appointment and promotion and the type of job security long enjoyed by civil servants, but will extend them to thousands of additional government employees. The Civil Service Commission is to become the public service commission and, within a wider jurisdiction, it is to be concerned exclusively with the staffing functions.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING FUNCTIONS OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the third of the bills necessarily arising out of the proposal for collective bargaining in the civil service. This particular bill proposes that Treasury Board be empowered to act for the governor in council on all matters relating to financial management, personnel management, general administrative policy, the organization of the public service and the control of establishments. In the personnel field the board would be responsible, among other things, for the determination of rates of pay, hours of work, leave and other conditions of employment; for the classification of positions and employees; for the establishment of standards of discipline; and for the promotion of safe and suitable working conditions.
The purpose of these provisions is to assign to Treasury Board the role envisaged for it by the Glassco commission and to provide it with the authority it will require to act as the principal agent of the employer in the proposed system of collective bargaining.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: FAILURE TO APPOINT CHAIRMAN FOR C.N.R. CONCILIATION BOARD
speechtext:
I am glad this question was put, because it gives me the opportunity to correct an erroneous statement which appeared in this morning's paper to the effect that the minister has neglected this matter for two months.
The facts are that it was on March 30 the union sent in its nomination. The company submitted its nomination on April 1. The parties were immediately advised by the minister, as required by the act, that they should get together and try to agree on a chairman. On April 19 I was advised they had not been able to agree. On the following day I announced the appointment of Mr. Justice Munroe to the chairmanship of the other two conciliation boards, and the hope was expressed that this particular union and the railways might be able to agree on his appointment in this case also. It was only, relatively, a short time ago that I was advised that this hope would not materialize.
Since then we have been actively exploring the possibilities because this is a very important matter. For the last ten days we have been trying to find another chairman, but bearing in mind the number of conciliation boards and other inquiries which are sitting at the present time hon. members will appreciate that it is not easy to get an experienced chairman to deal with a matter as complicated and as serious as this one.
We now have one experienced man in mind and I feel he could do the job well, if he will accept. He has promised to advise me tomorrow, if possible, or in any event not later than Monday, whether he will be able to take it on.

Mr. Speaker, last night at adjournment I had been speaking on matters pertaining to Bill No. C-151, which is now before us again. I had reminded the government of their unassumed and unadmitted responsibility for the current high cost of living which is a heavy burden particularly upon the older people and the poor people of our country, both rural and urban. I had also reminded the government to stay out of the real estate business and to forget their foolish election promise to buy up farms, create economic units and then sell them back to the farmers. I trust I made my point in this regard.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I had reminded the government of the support from farm organizations and the local press throughout Ontario that my argument is earning, particularly in my own area of Prince Edward-Lennox where the people still believe in private enterprise and the integrity and efforts of the individual. I reminded the government of the meeting of the Lennox and Addington Federation of Agriculture on April 26 at Napanee when that assembly was unanimous in declaring that rural development must start with the people.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that this meeting was also concerned about the retraining of rural people. I trust that this too is part of the intent and purpose of this bill, although retraining is not mentioned in any of its clauses. But I do note the cautionary attitude in clause 8, subclause 2, where the headlong rush into rural socialism is slightly checked in lines 5, 6 and 7 in that it provides that the advisory board shall recommend that the minister not enter into certain agreements regarding any program if in the opinion of the board the program can be carried out in another way without federal assistance.
Where federal assistance is needed and where the $50 million provided by the bill could well be spent-in fact, it would cost many times $50 million-is in the development of all our watersheds for the conservation of
(Mr. Pickersgill.l
clean water and in the reforestation of adaptable forest land in a productive manner to ensure continuance of the annual production of timber and wood products. This would involve a long term growth period before the realization of any profits.
Also, attention is needed in the areas of the watersheds I have mentioned where there is soil suitable for agriculture but requiring the clearing and restoration of old fields which formerly did produce something. Grants must be available toward the use of heavy machinery for clearing the jungles of scrub brush that have sprung up since many of these places were last occupied and cultivated. There should also be provision for tile drainage of these fields where this type of water control and drainage is necessary.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but in doing so I would only be repeating my remarks of last March. I have studied the briefs of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the National Farmers Union. Both strongly press for the stabilization of the agricultural industry through the preservation of productive family farming, but one significant qualification with regard to both briefs is that neither one of these great farm groups is pressing the government to buy farms, enlarge them into economic units at public expense and then sell these units back to the farmers. The farmers of Canada are too smart for that. The farmers of Canada will do their own developing of their own economic units and make their own real estate deals between themselves, between the farmer who is retiring and wants to get out of the business and his neighbour who wants to expand and strengthen his activities.
There is need also for thorough surveys of many areas and counties of Canada and, particularly in Ontario, surveys pertaining to the fiscal and sociological qualifications and aspects of the different regions.
Here, Mr. Speaker, is a timely resolution which I have received from Mr. G. M. Mills, agricultural representative for the county of Lennox and Addington and secretary of the ARDA committee for that county. I have sent a copy of this resolution to the minister who has very courteously acknowledged it. The resolution reads as follows:
The following motion was moved by Carl Clayton and seconded by Percy VanVlack that the Lennox and Addington ARDA committee suggests that a sociological survey of the county of Lennox and Addington, as outlined in the attached letter, be conducted and respectfully request the ARDA branch of the Ontario Department of Agriculture to engage the staff as required to conduct such a
May 12, 1966

survey in the summer of 1966 and that the survey be expanded to collect other information as may appear advisable, such as existing potential tourist development.
This motion was carried unanimously. I trust that the Lennox and Addington ARDA committee will obtain the desired services and co-operation from the provincial and federal bodies.
I have advised the minister on this matter and I thank him for the response I have received and for his written assurance that most of the objectives of the Lennox and Addington resolution will be adequately provided for by the survey under and application of the Canada land inventory program.
Many of us in this chamber, Mr. Speaker, have one thing in common. I point out that many hon. members are of rural origin and status. If it were not for the rural areas and the fact that originally a pastoral and agricultural civilization pioneered this country, our great cities and highly organized urban areas would not exist, and they could not continue to exist and grow today without the assistance of a vigorous agricultural industry.
We hear a lot about the family farm and we think a lot of the family farm. For many of us it is the dearest of our realities; for many of us it is the dearest of our memories. I am one of that number. I was born on an Algoma farm near Rydal Bank, Ontario, which is 10 miles north of Bruce Mines. My Scottish grandfather and grandmother made a fair living for a big family. My grandfather augmented that living with forest ranging in the summer. No one can make a living any more on that farm and the place is idle and deserted.
I also remember a farm in Kaladar township where my family lived. Kaladar township is only 100 miles west of Ottawa in the northern part of Lennox and Addington county. In the second decade of this century that farm, with its 250 acres of rough land, about 50 of which were tillable, produced a living for our family and no less than three hired men. Beef and dairy cattle were produced. Two large marshes that were on the property were cut each year to supplement winter feed. Lumbering and wood cutting were carried on, potatoes were a good cash crop and acres of turnips were grown each year on the sandy loam soil. However, what arable soil there was, as I said, was a sandy loam but it was kept productive by the steady annual application of large quantities of livestock manure.
Rural Development
Today that farm is deserted and unproductive. It fills me with nostalgic and wistful memories whenever I pass this place on Number 41 highway three miles north of Kaladar. True, the present owner has a tenant living in the house but the wind whistles through the rough, weathered vertical siding of the now long-empty barn that my father helped to build in the year 1911.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
This barn has a stone foundation, is of ample dimensions and stabled 60 head of cattle. I would say it stored at least 60 tons of hay. I have heard hon. members say that such areas which cannot now maintain production should never have been cleared for agriculture. I grant that this is probably true. In that particular area at one time some of the finest pine timber in the country grew, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Hopkins) who represents a similar area. Man's personal greed, which resulted in a lack of conservation policies in the early days, and the cross-cut saw have been the undoing of this area. I might say that in 1920 my family moved to Napanee, a more productive part of the country, and settled in Richmond township.
Some of the examples I have mentioned, for which I can personally vouch, as well as many others across the country will provide the areas in which this measure must work and work according to the principles of ARDA. As we approach Canada's second century I predict that if ARDA makes a proper start the men sitting here 100 years from now will still be using ARDA and its fundamental principles to improve and rehabilitate the forgotten and neglected corners of Canada.
Let us go back momentarily to the term "economic unit", about which we hear so much. I should like to quote the Rural CoOperator's definition of an economic farm unit. This article appeared in the Rural CoOperator for Tuesday, April 26, 1966, under the heading, "There's A Future On Such a Farm".
What is the future of the 150 to 200 acre dairy farm? From time to time some economists predict the demise of this type of operation within 10 to 20 years. They urge the creation of enormous enterprises such as the big corporation farm. Largeness is equated with efficiency.
You can put a big question mark after that statement, Mr. Speaker. There is a great deal of doubt now that largeness is equated with efficiency. I continue to quote:
However, over the past two or three years a number of intensive studies have been completed on

May 12, 19B6
Rural Development
what constitutes the efficient farming unit. Michigan research workers concluded that the ideal size of the family farming unit ranged between just below 200 acres and up to 300 acres.
Farms above this range run into problems such as under use of equipment and shortages of hired help. And with really large units, there was the very real problem of finding workers who would take a personal interest in livestock operations.
This article bears out my warning to the government as to the variation in the requirements for economic units in the various areas across the country. In addition, this statement is borne out by the fact that rural people and bona fide farmers are the best judges of the application of the term "economic unit" as it may apply to future operations.
There is another cautionary note to be injected here which I take from that very extensive preliminary report on rural poverty in four selected areas of our country. This report was prepared by the Canadian Welfare Council and I should like to congratulate its compilers and editors upon the valuable information they have provided. As a result of interviews with dozens of families living in varying degrees of economic circumstances in the four selected areas of Canada, it is to be noted that almost without exception the head of the family said that despite the existing disadvantages he did not wish to leave his farm. I again warn the government not to create a situation in which rural people are uprooted and forced into an urban environment for which they are ill-suited and unadaptable. In short, there are certain types of people who would rather live on the land than anywhere else despite their economic problems. This is their right, their liberty and, moreover, a good philosophy of life.
This statement applies especially to parents who do not want to move at middle age. Let us agree to use the $50 million to help them stay there, to help them produce something tangible where very little was produced before. Let us help them to help themselves.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT OF SPECIAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say something in this debate I want to say that, unlike most of the members who have participated in the discussion, I do not represent a rural area. However, I do represent a constituency in which I have met a large number of people who have moved from rural areas in Manitoba, particularly from the Interlake area of which the minister spoke the other day. Before I became a federal member I represented a provincial constituency in

which there were a large number of Indian and Metis people who came to the city of Winnipeg from the reserves on which they had lived with their families for generations. I am in favour of improving the living conditions of people who have traditionally lived in the rural areas of this country. One could no more oppose this bill than one could get up in this house and say he was opposed to motherhood.
At the same time I am not at all convinced from what I have heard or what I have read that there is anything in this bill which will do much except move the people who now live in the rural slums of Canada into the urban slums of Canada. There is not much advantage to a person moving from one slum to another. I am not convinced they will live much better in the urban slums of Winnipeg, Toronto or Montreal than they have in the rural slums. This is a tremendous problem with which this bill proposes to deal. In introducing the measure on May 10, the minister gave some very interesting figures. He pointed out that in this country there are over 95,000 families living on farms which could be classified as low income farms. This meant that they had gross sales of less than $2,500 a year. He spoke of the Interlake area of Manitoba in which there are almost 3,500 farms and in which one-third of the farms sell annually between $1,200 and $2,500 worth of products. The remaining 40 per cent sell less than $1,200 worth of products annually, e (4:00 p.m.)
I have been in that area and I know the conditions under which the people live. I can remember canvassing in the Selkirk constituency and being in a town in which the people were living in tarpaper shacks. Indeed, the wallpaper consisted of old copies of the Winnipeg Free Press. I cannot think of a better use for copies of the Winnipeg Free Press than that very practical use but it is not very esthetic wallpaper, to put it mildly. Nobody in this house is going to object to this bill under which it is proposed to spend $50 million. However, when one looks at the rural problem, when one realizes that as careful an observer as Mr. Merrill Menzies, who worked very closely with the minister of agriculture in the former government, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), and I think is still doing some work for this government, says that in order to put in a program that will have any hope of success we will probably need to think in terms of spending not $50 million but $1,500 million, then one can
May 12, 1966

see we are really only beginning to nibble at the edges of the problem.
I am wondering what the minister proposes to do under this bill which could not have been done under earlier legislation such as P.F.R.A. I am not being critical; I think these things need to be done. But what the minister is proposing to do under this bill is to improve the physical-the minister shakes his head. If I am wrong I hope that some time he will explain why. The minister is proposing to improve the physical use of the land. He proposes to buy out farmers who are living on holdings which are too small for them, to consolidate farm holdings and help the farmers plant trees which will later be used for pulp and paper.
That is all very well, Mr. Speaker, but there is nothing in the bill, and I could find nothing in what the minister said in introducing the bill or anything he said earlier, which would indicate to me that the minister has come up with a plan to rehabilitate the human beings who are affected by rural poverty and who will be moved under the legislation now proposed. It seems obvious to me that the important thing is to do something not about the existing physical conditions but about the human beings who are involved.
We are still talking, Mr. Speaker, about test areas. This question was raised by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schreyer) when he spoke a few days ago. How long must we go on testing? How long must we go on trying before we decide that the program is workable and can be implemented to the benefit of all concerned?
I am informed that some of the surveys of projects commenced several years ago, now completed but not yet published, indicate that the people who were moved as a result of these earlier projects are no better off now than they were before. I would be interested to hear the minister tell the house, either during this debate or on discussion of his estimates, of actual cases where the program has rehabilitated groups of farmers who have been relocated. If that information is available I think it should be given to the members of the house and the public as a whole.
It seems to me that this legislation is not broad enough to provide for a comprehensive program of rehabilitation of the sort required. If I am wrong I should like to hear from the minister where such a program is spelled out in this bill or in anything which he said.
Rural Development
During the conference on poverty which was called by the government some months ago a paper was presented by the special planning secretariat entitled "Profile Of Poverty In Canada'" This paper was referred to by my colleague, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), during the Budget debate. In discussing what should be done about poverty the paper made a number of practical suggestions. It suggested that we would have to deal with the question of education, with the question of housing and with the question of health; yet none of these matters are dealt with in this bill.
It may be that the minister will answer that these questions will be dealt with in the manpower program of the government or in the proposal for a health insurance program. But I would submit that this whole program will fall apart and will be unsuccessful unless the basic factors I have just mentioned are dealt with, and they are not dealt with at the present time.
I want to summarize very briefly what the "Profile of Poverty" report to the conference on poverty suggested. With regard to education it stated:
A I960 survey showed that about half of the unemployed had not finished primary school. Over 90 per cent had not completed high school. Among people who had not completed primary school, the unemployment rate was six times greater than it was among high school graduates.
A little farther on there is this paragraph:
The child of poor parents is greatly handicapped in taking advantage of the educational system. It assumes of him values and experience that he often does not have. Poor housing (which means lack of facilities for study), ill health, poor social and home environment, distance to school, lack of proper nourishment and clothing, ignorance of opportunities, as well as psychological factors and the attractiveness of early earnings-all these are reasons why poor children tend to drop out of school earlier and therefore why a culture of poverty tends to be perpetuated.
That statement was reinforced by the minister the other day when he gave the percentage of rural population of school age or over, but not attending school, whose highest grade attended was grade 8 or less. It appears, according to the figures put on the record by the minister, that in every province in Canada more than 50 per cent of the rural population-in Quebec it was 77 per cent and in Newfoundland 72 per cent-have not attended school beyond the level of grade eight. Under these circumstances, what the minister proposes to do here is bound to fail regardless of how aggressively he proceeds with the

May 12. 1966
Rural Development
program. The "Profile of Poverty in Canada" paper, dealing with the question of health, had this to say:
Low income groups receive less health care than higher income groups, although they suffer from more illnesses in general and their illnesses tend to be more severe.
Assistance in meeting health needs has so far been of benefit more to the elderly than to other people. That is, the gap in treatment between poor children and rich children is greater than the gap between the aged poor and the aged affluent.
These people are concentrated to a large extent in the areas with which the bill proposes to deal, but they can look forward to very little as a result of the proposal of the minister.
With regard to housing the report had this to say:
In 1961 Canadian housing provided one-third more rooms than the number of people. But in 60,000 homes there were only half as many rooms as people.
Crowding as measured by persons per room is closely linked to income levels. Among families earning $6,000 and over in 1961, only 18 per cent lived in dwellings providing less than a room per person. Among families earning less than $3,000, this proportion was 35 per cent.
It is no secret that the majority of the people living in rural areas, particularly the kind of areas this bill is supposed to assist, are people who live in homes not equipped with running water or indoor plumbing, and have only the barest minimum living conditions which could be considered at all adequate. There is nothing in this bill to indicate that the government proposes to make a major drive toward improving the housing conditions of those who live in the rural and undeveloped areas of this country.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
In the pamphlet entitled "Poverty In Canada" by Mr. M. W. Menzies, to which I referred earlier, mention is made of what the problem is and what needs to be done. I want to summarize this very briefly. It seems to me that Mr. Menzies has indicated both the problem and the solution. The minister seems to have paid attention to the problem. I do not think, however, from anything the minister has said that it can be shown that he has thought of the solutions pointed out by Mr. Menzies and other serious thinkers to the problem of rehabilitating the rural poor. Nothing that the minister has said would indicate that he is thinking along these lines.

I quote briefly from page 6 of the pamphlet by Mr. Menzies:
Approximately 50 per cent of the farmers in the study area, if provided with suitable alternative employment and the training required for it, could leave the agricultural industry to the benefit of themselves and to the net gain of the remaining farm community and the national economy.
I am sure the minister would agree with that, as would every other hon. member of this house. However, unless we do a great deal in the way of education not only for those who are now in schools but for those who did not attend school or who did not attain more than a grade 8 education-in the case of Indians this would apply to those who do not have more than a grade 4 education- and are moving into the cities of Canada, the proposals which the minister and the government have made will come to naught. We must inaugurate an aggressive program of adult education.
I know the difficulties. I know that education is a provincial responsibility. However, unless the federal government takes the lead in working out a co-operative program of education with the provinces, the problem which this bill seeks to solve and the problem of manpower, the solution of which required the appointment of a new minister with a galaxie of civil servants backing him up, will fail to be solved. Although the level of education has improved in my own and in other provinces it is still so low that a crash education program is required at this time. Nothing that I have heard from the Minister of Forestry or from any other minister indicates that the government is trying to solve the problems I have just outlined.
Mr. Menzies also says on page 7:
Relatively few farmers in any of the study areas who owned less than 100 improved acres had achieved an economic farm operation.
I suppose the minister will say that is precisely what this program is designed to do, to consolidate land holding so that farmers will have more than 100 acres. If that is intended I suppose that the program may be successful. However, I am very concerned about those who will be forced off the land and probably move into cities such as Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal, Regina or Calgary and who will, for the reasons I have already indicated, not be sufficiently equipped by way of education or experience, or because of their whole way of life previously, to make a go of it in the city. It seems to me that we must develop a program to help people who
May 12, 1966

move from the rural areas to the city, as they are doing.
Mr. Menzies points out that almost half of the cash receipts of farmers with farm incomes of less than $2,500 came from off-farm earnings and from such social payments as family allowances, old age pensions, welfare payments and the like. When it comes to the Indians, I submit that the proportion of income derived in that way would be not half but three-quarters or more. Here again, I submit that we must devise programs in order to help those people to become self-sustaining, and to help them come off the welfare rolls. In that way they would no longer be a charge on the state, a charge on the community, but instead would become selfsufficient, independent and be able to manage for themselves as do most people in Canada.
I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, that I am not an expert. It is not my intention to oppose or vote against the bill. It seems to me that behind this bill, as behind the proposal for the Company of Young Canadians, we have a slogan picked up by the Prime Minister and by other ministers from President Johnson of the United States who used the famous phrase "the war on poverty." The war on poverty in this country is probably the most important war we can fight and .should be fighting.
The Prime Minister picked up this slogan about two and a half years ago. Canada was going to have its own war on poverty. I do mot want to be critical of the Company of Young Canadians. It may very well be a good program. However, one would have thought when the Prime Minister first announced the war on poverty some two and a half years ago that there would have been activity in the field within days or weeks. Yet two and a half years have gone by and still the program is in the planning stage. It is the same, I submit, with this program which is a new version of ARDA. It is the same with the other war on poverty programs so far announced by the government.
What we have had so far is a fantastic deluge of words. If every word uttered by the Prime Minister, other cabinet ministers and other members of the Liberal party who have spoken about the war on poverty in the last two and a half years were worth $1, we should have more than enough money to solve the problems of poverty in this country. I hope that we have had enough words from the government side and that we will see ;some action. I hope that as the result of the
Rural Development
wonderfully enthusiastic speeches made by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Forestry and other ministers we shall begin to solve the problem of the poor in Canada instead of merely talking about it. We must admit with a good deal of shame in this year of affluence, 1966, that the poor still comprise more than a quarter of the people of Canada. That is not good enough.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT OF SPECIAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the speeches which have been made on this ARDA matter. I must say that, even though the speeches were not of equal value, I have learned something useful about the proposed legislation from all of them. This applies more specifically to the statement made by the hon. minister at the beginning of the debate.
Some of the things the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has just said are quite accurate, and I agree with him on some of them. For instance, there is a pressing need to foster education in Canada, within the limits, naturally, of the constitution. However, I did find the tone of his speech rather pessimistic, and feel that this legislation, although it is far from perfect or adequate, will still be of great use to the country.
I should like to point out, in answer to an objection raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, when he said that the government seems to have been fumbling around in the last two years or two and a half years and that it talks a lot about proposed legislation but does not accomplish very much, that as an independent I do not have a political party to protect or destroy. To my mind- and I bring up a matter I have already mentioned two or three times in the house-if we could but have a truce for a few months and postpone our petty personal and political wrangling, say till after the summer recess, in order to pass the series of bills we have been promised in the last year or two, and if there were to be less filibustering from some parties in the house, it would be possible to have a greater number of laws beneficial to the Canadian people generally. This is intended to be constructive criticism on my part.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, I think we have had a constructive debate up to now and it should be carried on in that spirit. The way in which the minister introduced his bill has

May 12, 1966
Rural Development
probably a great deal to do with the constructive aspect of the debate. He was not so narrow-minded as to claim all the credit for himself or his party, but gave due credit to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) who introduced this legislation when he was minister of agriculture. In short, he explained his bill in a way which contributed to maintain the serenity of the house.
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to give the impression that I am just saying this to make a speech; I simply want to point out to the house that this tone should be more generally adopted when we are considering a piece of legislation.
I have been very much interested in this bill from the beginning and, even if I do not represent an essentially rural constituency, I have studied the bill because I was one of the founders of the Central Quebec Mayors Conference which is interested in the economy of the region known as the Mauricie.
I have also studied the bill because I am a former member of the executive of the Canadian Federation of Mayors which contributed to the creation of an organization known as the Canadian Council for Urban and Rural Renewal which is particularly interested in area planning.
Even if all the possibilities of the bill are not as familiar to me as they are to the experts, I would like nevertheless to submit two cases to the minister, two cases in point or pilot cases, as it were, which I think would perhaps also help other areas to better understand the possibilities of the bill.
My own constituency is semi-rural and semi-urban. In the rural part, including the municipalities of Saint-Etienne-des-Gres, Saint-Barnabe, Pointe-du-Lac, Saint-Thomas-de-Caxton, and a part of Yamachiche, there are extremely poor farms.
A century or a century and a half ago people settled there because it was a good lumber area and they prospered. However, in the past 30 or 40 years, the farms have become quite marginal, but they could easily be improved and thousands of acres could thus be redeveloped, near cities, into very profitable truck farms. This would keep on the farm thousands of farmers and sons of farmers now going to the city and taking up the jobs of city people.
After a brief study, we thought of a solution, and I wonder if ARDA could not help implement this solution in order to redevelop all those farms.

Here is the solution. The Union of Municipalities and Mayors of the province of Quebec, in co-operation with the Central Quebec Mayors Conference, thought at one point that the domestic garbage disposal system, producing compost, could be useful. The provincial government participated in this study by sending a delegation to Europe to see how this system could be used to make a sort of compost which would be very advantageously used to improve marginal farms when fertilizer is also added. In any case, that is the opinion of farm experts.
In my area, if I may be allowed to mention it, Trois-Rivieres, Trois-Rivieres-Ouest, Pointe-du-Lac, there are several small municipalities where garbage serves no useful purpose. It is sent to the incinerator for burning, whereas each day tons of domestic garbage could be treated with the bacteriological process and turned into compost which could be used as a fertilizer.
It is a project that would probably cost $750,000 to serve not only the whole territory of Trois-Rivieres itself but also a large area of the province of Quebec.
That project was studied quite a bit. I am wondering if it would not be possible to carry it out with the help of the municipalities? The government of the province of Quebec which studied the problem seems ready to do its share through its Department of Agriculture and its Department of Commerce and Industry. Moreover, I am wondering if it would not be possible to have a more detailed study made by technicians to submit that project to the province. I am telling this to the minister to find out if it might not come under the scope of the ARDA program. In my opinion, it would help solve an acute rural problem in the riding which interests me personally.
But my preoccupations go outside the riding of Trois-Rivieres, Mr. Speaker, and here is why. I am a director of what is called the tourist board of the St. Maurice region, which is made up of some 85 municipalities in central Quebec and sponsored by some 80 mayors who are themselves members of the Mayors' Conference of central Quebec which merged, a year or two ago, with the tourist organization which covers the region served by the Lake St. John-Roberval highway.
I think that from the municipality called Les Piles, a little further North of Grand'Mere, which is now part of the St. Maurice riding but which, after redistribution, will be in the riding of Champlain-and I
May 12. 1966

am grateful to my colleague for the riding of Champlain (Mr. Matte) for saying a word about it the other day in his speech-that area is now almost unproductive from an agricultural point of view. As a matter of fact, it is too hilly, too rocky. But it is wonderful country for tourists. It has a very good road which follows the St. Maurice river in a colourful setting; I would say it is even more colourful than what can be seen north of Montreal, and it reminds one of the Matapedia valley.
Some of the land there is unsuitable for farming because it is too rough and the farms are unproductive because the region is too mountainous. These people go to work in the towns or in the bush.
This territory is almost 70 miles long. Mr. Speaker, I should like to repeat, with your permission, what I said earlier about the hon. member for Champlain, who was absent at the time. I would like to thank him again for his intervention the other day concerning this area which will soon be part of the riding of Champlain.
Sheep and goat breeding could be promoted, since the region is mountainous; this is also a branch of farming, but I am less familiar with it and I shall not pursue the subject.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
But there could be a further development of the tourist industry, which is already promising and for which private industry and municipalities have made great sacrifice. It could be expanded considerably, since the trans-Canada highway will go through La Tuque, Grand-Mere and Shawinigan. And, all the local people of those territories could stay on their land and would not be forced to go to cities to take up the jobs of city people, or to go to work in the bush. This would kill two birds with one stone. It would open up jobs for unemployed city people, and these country people could live in their territories. Private enterprise has been able to do something. Municipalities took an interest in it. If it were possible to get some assistance from ARDA to complete what has been done by the public bodies up to now, it would mean the development of a potentially rich economic area in central Quebec.
Studies were carried out, but they were summary studies. In 1961, the Quebec government let us have technicians on loan through the Department of Commerce and Industry. They loaned us economists. They prepared a survey of the potential of the
Rural Development
area, which was incorporated in an interesting volume which I will be pleased to forward to the minister in a couple of days and which can be used as a working basis for more extensive studies.
The time has come to give a definite stimulus to all these things for which the mayors, the members of parliament, the tourist commissioners and the Quebec department of commerce and industry paved the way.
Preliminary studies are costly. The services of experts in all kinds of disciplines are required. I think ARDA can support the cost of such preliminary studies. But you will understand that there are two objections: The time needed by the province to approve the projects and the time needed by the federal government to give confirmation will delay the projects quite a bit. Municipalities are sometimes reluctant to embark upon such a project, before knowing what it may represent.
The minister can clarify the situation concerning the problems which I raise and which are similar to those raised here during the discussions. Will ARDA participate only in cases under the jurisdiction of the municipality or under that of the farmers co-operative? Or will ARDA participate in certain cases where private interest could also be involved? Those are questions to which I have no answer, and which could help solve our problem.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this ARDA program is outstanding. We talk of fighting against poverty. There is a concrete way of doing it. Readers of Time magazine will see what tribulations are being experienced in the United States in their war against poverty. They will see that Canada is directing its efforts much more realistically and that, in so doing, it will escape the trials and bitter criticism experienced by the Americans.
I congratulate the hon. minister and his colleagues who have created this body.
Before resuming my seat, in accord with the member for Champlain, I should like to urge the minister to meet the Central Quebec Mayors' Conference and the St. Maurice Tourist Commission which deal with the problems I have just mentioned. He will be asked questions. He will find people there who are willing to co-operate in the implementation of measures intended to make poverty and misery vanish from our midst.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT OF SPECIAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house is now studying Bill

May 12, 1966
Rural Development
C-151, an act to provide for the establishment of a fund for the economic and social development of special rural development areas. As for special areas, I think there are several of them in Canada. There is scope for specializing a little everywhere. But I fail to understand this, Mr. Speaker, that in the 20th century, in 1966, in a world of progress and development, in which political and scientific economics has developed in every field, we should be waging a war on poverty.
We should not have to speak of poverty in 1966, in a century of progress and science: but the system or industry throws the Canadian people in such poverty and destitution as has not been known anywhere in the world.
Possibilities are numerous in Canada. The physical possibilities are tremendous, but the financial possibilities are not there. The financial possibilities do not reflect the physical realities in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, before going further, I should like to see, to get a picture of what ARDA should do. The minister has spoken about it. He has outlined ARDA. I would like to tell the house what responsibilities the ARDA program should consider.
Mr. Speaker, there was, there is still much room for improvement, especially in agriculture, since ARDA is intended to help agriculture; this does not mean that it should help only agriculture and not the other fields. Already, $125 million have been voted, and spent, I believe, without giving anything much to agriculture; indeed, without improving anything very much in other sectors of the Canadian and Quebec economy.
So, we are asked to approve another amount of $50 million. I feel that $50 million is but a drop in the bucket. What are we going to do with $50 million to restore the economy of a country with 20 million people? Mr. Speaker, it would take two billion dollars just to start on an economically feasible basis with a plan such as that one. We talk of $50 million, when there are physical possibilities for two billion dollars. But we lack the financial resources to finance the developments or improvements everyone would like to see springing up.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, here again there has been a lack of research from a technical standpoint on agricultural methods, farm land possibilities, farm management and marketing. This has been lacking and it still is. This is

where ARDA should spend its money if we really want to help agriculture to come out of its stagnation.
A bigger slice of the ARDA budget should therefore be devoted to research and experimentation and to further the knowledge of those whose task it is to improve agricultural science and techniques.
There should be a greater number of true specialists for most types of farming.
ARDA should see to it that farming techniques are rationally put into use according to rural resources available and their development, whether it is the human potential or physical resources, or any means the farmer has to produce.
A farmer may be relatively efficient on his farm and even successful to some extent without making full use of the resources available to him; either his resources are limited or they are fully used or, still, poorly used.
I understand that the objective of ARDA is, of course, to get maximum production from existing resources; this is the objective.
One look at official statistics, Mr. Speaker, will suffice to ascertain the seriousness of the stagnation in the field of agriculture at the present time.
We are told that this amount is needed to take agriculture and the Canadian economy out of their present stagnation.
The gap between the cost of services and technical equipment, on the one hand, and the prices of farm products paid to farmers, on the other hand, is increasing. Prices in general have remained unchanged since 1949 while cost of goods and services has steadily increased.
The net margin of profit, per production unit, has therefore decreased. It is not surprising, therefore, that the purchasing power of farm products as compared to the price of farm equipment has decreased by close to 28 per cent during the 1949-1963 period.
It is to be noted that the cost of living has increased considerably on the farm-by about 75 per cent-during the same period. Furthermore, the producer's share of the consumer dollar has been decreasing all the time. In 1950, the Canadian farmer was getting 50 cents out of the consumer's dollar, but in 1960 he was only getting 40 cents and in 1964, 35 cents.
The actual net farm income has decreased considerably since 1949, taking into account
May 12, 1966

the fact that the number of farms has also decreased, and this shows the tragic situation of Quebec agriculture.
There have only been a few good years for our farmers during that period. For instance, during the period 1951-1955, the national average net farm income was $237 million, but in the past few years, it has remained between $185 and $200 million. We had the opposite situation in the larger cities where, since 1949, the purchasing power of the other classes of society has increased by at least 51 to 52 per cent.
According to statistics, in 1963 the average weekly salary of industrial workers in Montreal was $82.43, while the average net income of the farmer for the same year was $2,100, that is $40 per week. This income covered his work and that of his family and paid off his debts.
This does not mean that our farming is inefficient; on the contrary, agricultural production has practically doubled over the last 15 years or so, in spite of a noticeable labour reduction of almost 50 per cent. We should therefore recognize that others have profited from the efforts of the farmers to increase their production and their efficiency; product quality standards, processing and distribution standards have been raised; only one factor has been forgotten, consumer prices. It is not abnormal that the farmer, who is first in production, should become the last one considered with regard to remuneration? When considering the farmer in an industrial context, one is constantly faced with paradoxes.
Indeed, he is ostentatiously called a contractor, when his income puts him in the same class as the most disfavoured workers.
This small income is further reduced by the property tax, which in 1963 represented about 9 per cent of the gross income. To this could be added the tax on building materials, representing an additional disbursement of at least 17 per cent: 11 per cent for the federal government and 6 per cent for the provincial government.
This is the situation in which our farmers find themselves. If we are really to help agriculture, to fight poverty, we must eliminate this precious 11 per cent tax which is ruining the farmers and destroying his spirit of enterprise.
High finance controls all our institutions, both agricultural and commercial, as well as transportation.
Rural Development
The ARDA program will socialize our countryside.
Farm credit, that is to say farmers in debt, is the very cause of the destruction of the farming community.
Grants to institutions are paralysing resistance.
Taxes are ruining us; they are one of the factors which have paralysed our farmers through spoliation and mortgages on their property.
School taxes in the country have become an intolerable burden to farmers with a small annual income of $1,500 to $2,000 for the whole family. They have to pay $400 to $500 a year in school taxes, not to mention municipal taxes and the interest on their farm loans. They have nothing left to live on for themselves and their families; that is why they abandon their farms and go to the cities.
All sorts of other ways are tried to live in the city. I will tell you frankly, Mr. Speaker, that many of the farmers are unhappy in the city because they are made to live out in the country; they would like to live on farms, but they do not have the means to go back or to make a living there.
Farmers once had large families, made a good living from their farms, and the father could even help his sons to settle on a neighbouring farm; his daughters were also helped. The opposite is true today.
With modern progress, life in the country has become impossible. It is easy to understand why.
The ministers and the economists long-windedly try to prove that farming is not, or is no longer profitable and that only the state can afford to farm.
I should like to ask these ministers and economists how it is that in some countries, carrots can be grown on rocks. Rocks are being cultivated. Such rocks are being planted and become profitable. In Canada, we have the most productive farms anywhere in the world and they are abandoned.
How is it that farms are no longer profitable or, if so, only to the few?
A farmer requesting a farm loan is told: "Your farm is not economic, give it up and go to the city." The farm is sold to the second neighbour. How is it that it is not economic for one but it is for the other?

May 12, 1966
Rural Development
This is the situation which prevails now in the province of Quebec. I do not know much about the other provinces but I imagine the situation is about the same.
Our producers are the victims of all kinds of regulations which compel them to equip themselves beyond their means, to give milk control to a group of friends in the government or to financial backers of elections.
It is true that the Farm Credit Act has temporarily alleviated the lot of the farmers, but it is or was credit to repay. If our economists and our governments had opened their eyes and their ears, they would not have prepared the way so well for socialists and communists, against whom they are trying to fight.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
What is needed is interest-free credit to finance the producers, farmers and others; it is interest-free loans from the Bank of Canada or credit offices. Interest-free loans are free money for development. It is not with interest-ridden money, borrowed money or debt money that the economy can be improved.
If only our federal and provincial governments had listened to the voice of the Credi-tistes and created credit, they would have helped the farmers more than with their miserable farm credit or the ARDA program. It is a sleeping pill and when the poor sleeper awakens, he finds out that he has been stripped for everything he had; interest on his loan and taxes have left him nothing. That is why he has to leave his farm. Taxes have increased in proportion to the improvement of the farm or industry. Your farm is valued at $6,000 and you mortgage it for $4,000, but the municipal assessors are kind enough to assess your property at $13,000 and the taxes get higher and higher. Several people know that story because it happened to them.
What drove the farmers away from the rural areas? The present system. And as a remedy, socialism is forced upon us by laws which will impoverish the community even more and will leave the citizens poorer and poorer and stripped of their heritage.
What we need is not credit with interest; mortgages in a stifling financial system or grants to the socialists of the ARDA program are not what will save us; it is the liberating social credit with interest-free loans for producers and free money for consumers.
That is what would save us, Mr. Speaker.

They are creating socialism which will take over because individuals cannot live on their own under the present system. The state is socialization, control.
Mr. Speaker, with an upside-down and unhealthy financial system such as the one we have, socialism is inevitable, people are starving.
Take the school boards for instance. They no longer can meet their obligations in the rural areas and in the cities; they are no longer able to balance their budget; therefore, they ask for grants; the grants are never unconditional and the conditions are control by inspectors, strait-jackets.
Communism sets in. Loss of freedom ensues. Public debt increases, taxes become general and, soon, citizens receive only the stubs of their cheques. That is where the present system is leading us, because our leaders refuse to assume their responsibilities to put some order in the financial system and socialize credit instead of socializing goods and individuals. Those are our responsibilities.
As the country develops, our debts progress and increase: personal debts, federal debts, provincial debts, school debts, hospital debts, university debts-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your remarks and I shall certainly follow your suggestion.
Since the bill deals with money, one must refer to money matters. In that case, the discussion turns to administration; when one speaks about administration, one must refer to taxes, debts and the present situation. That is why I mentioned the present indebtedness and imbalance in various fields. It is impossible to survive, to progress and to operate with money as is being done, while turning everything over to the administration. I know that out of the $50 million for ARDA, three quarters will go for administration costs and approximately one quarter for the development of the ARDA program. That is why I say $2 billion would be needed instead of $50 million. What can be done with $50 million? It is ridiculous to vote $50 million in order to teach how to fight poverty and to strengthen the economy of a country.
I know that progress is made according to one's resources not according to opportunities. There are many opportunities, but they refuse to issue the money possible to develop those opportunities in Canada. That is why I want to try and make some people understand that no economic progress is possible if our financial system is not adjusted to our economy.
When an area is developed, it is merely a physical and material development; if no financial development takes place, the results are not worthwhile.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Finance is needed to operate. If we can produce goods in Canada, we can also produce finance. If we do not do so, it is 23033-3201
Rural Development
because we refuse to accept our responsibilities. There, Mr. Speaker, is the crux of the problem.
Now, taxes make taxes, and taxes make more debts. What do the financiers give in sweat for the millions they lend the government and individuals? Not a single drop. They only supply drops of ink. That sums up the question of finance; it is nothing else. Finance is a matter of accounting: accounting means balancing. Accounting must be adapted to facts and reality, as well as to the physical possibilities Canada holds. That is where we stand, Mr. Speaker.
Now, before bringing my remarks to a close, I should like to refer to the answer the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Berger) gave me yesterday in reply to my question. He said it was always the same story, a question of finance, it was this or that. If it is not a matter of finance, what is it? Why $50 million, Mr. Speaker, if it is not a question of finance? Why give out money, then levy taxes? All this concerns finance.
But I say taxes rob the people. Those who lend money and credit dominate through their power and have reduced the government or governments to mere servants of private interests. That is the point we have reached: we have become mere servants of private interests. Yet, we are able to govern. We should be at the controls; others should not come from St. James Street in Montreal, or Bay Street in Toronto. Orders should come from Parliament, from the Minister of Finance. He is in charge, he holds the controls; in short, he holds everything; he could, if he wanted to, with the approval of the Canadian people and the members of Parliament, organize, even tomorrow morning, a viable economy in Canada, an economy of prosperity in affluence.
We know how to produce. There is no difficulty in that respect. If you want production, it is yours for the asking. If you need a pig, Mr. Minister, you will have one. There is no need of a plan for this and a plan for that, or any other gimmick. The people want to know. And we are the ones who know nothing about finance. We do not know what to do with finance. When someone puts the matter before us, we find that funny. It is funny for the moment, but it will not always be funny; let us keep that in mind.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT OF SPECIAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before closing the debate on second reading, let me thank the 29 members who, since Tuesday, have made very interesting comments on the bill itself, on the ARDA program or on the situation in rural areas.
As you can well understand, I followed with great attention everything that was said.
I could easily answer every question put to me but I believe it might perhaps be preferable if I confined myself to five or six basic points raised by several members.
Much was said about the fact that, in my introductory remarks, I mentioned only three special development areas.
In fact, I wanted to give only three examples of the kind of comprehensive development program we could have. There are a great many other areas in each of the provinces of Canada, and discussions are now under way with the provinces in connection with the establishment of special development areas.
I am thinking, for instance, of the census districts Nos. 14 and 15, in Alberta, northern Saskatchewan as well as Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Cape Breton, and New Brunswick. I did not want to talk at length of all areas in which we are now making development plans, in conjunction with the provinces, because it seemed to me it would lengthen this debate much too much.
I gave only three examples to give an indication of how we see the job.
I think it is very important, first of all, to emphasize the method used, the procedure followed. It is the provincial government which designates, with the federal government, through, the administration of ARDA, a special development area, under Part VI of the ARDA agreement.
Once an area is designated and once the method of financing preliminary studies is estabished, a comprehensive area development program is prepared.
Why do we propose to aim at certain areas of Canada, excluding others? Simply because we, in the provincial and federal governments, thought that a very special effort is needed where low-income families are concentrated in rural areas.

And the program we are proposing under Bill C-151 is meant to enable the federal government to make a special financial effort in those areas.
Remember that there is the federal-provincial agreement on the economic rehabilitation of rural areas which covers all the rural areas in Canada and does not exclude anything; that this agreement was signed by all the provinces at the beginning of 1965 and that the federal government undertook to allocate to it $125 million in the next five years; the provinces will probably allocate a similar amount to it.
But, in addition to that program, and in any case that is provided for in the agreement I have just mentioned, in Part VI, paragraph 37, there is something about the creation of a special fund and Bill C-151 which we are considering today concerns that fund.
Nothing is excluded in the sense that under the general ARDA program there can be programs for land redevelopment, rehabilitation and consolidation of farms, drainage, water conservation.
But, under Bill C-151 and Part VI of the agreement, the federal government and the provinces can agree to make a special effort in some areas.
Therefore, the procedure is practically the same as for the other parts of the ARDA agrement, except that a considerable financial effort is believed to be needed in certain areas.

Many members have mentioned that the $50 million provided by this fund will not be enough. I completely agree with them. However, it seems necessary to start with a fund and the proposal is that as soon as the sum of $50 million has been committed we will then come back to parliament to secure more funds. We could have asked for $100 million or $150 million but we felt that the initial amount of $50 million would give us an opportunity to see how the provinces would decide to co-operate with the federal government in the implementation of special rural development plans. These plans will apply particularly to human resources. Under the general ARDA agreement we cover the physical resources, but we are conscious that in some low income areas of this country there are problems of education, housing and health. The speakers this afternoon and in the last few days have insisted upon the necessity of better plans for education and housing conditions, with which we all agree.
May 12, 1966



We will soon be releasing some of the special agreements which we are now discussing with the provinces and they will show a special effort on the part of the federal government in co-operation with the provinces to get at the heart of the problems. I cannot give more details this afternoon because we have not yet finalized these programs. However, when this announcement is released to the public, members of parliament will see that we are making a special effort under this rural development program which will affect the well-being of individuals and not concentrate so much on the physical resources of the various regions.
In no case under Bill No. C-151 or the old agreements under ARDA is there any compulsory method to buy land nobody is forced to sell his land. In any event, it is always the provinces who take the initiative of proposing farm programs to the federal government for consideration. There is no threat of compulsion. Nobody is being asked to sell unless he wants to sell for one reason or another. There is no question of expropriation; there is no program for the establishment of state farms and so on.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In clause 7 of the bill there is mention of an advisory council. It is to be a council composed of high civil servants in Ottawa to review the programs which will be drafted by the ARDA administration in co-operation with the provinces. It is an administrative body only. There is already in existence under the general ARDA statute, in accordance with the provision of clause 7, a Canadian Council for Rural Development which supervises developments under ARDA agreements made in accordance with either Bill No. C-152 or Bill No. C-151. On this council there are representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the National Farmers Union, the Canadian Welfare Council, the Canadian Forestry Association, and the like. We have popular representation on this council which will allow the ARDA administration to have contact with people in rural areas or people who are mostly concerned with rural development.
We do not intend to increase the staff of ARDA to implement the terms of Bill No. C-151 because most of the work is done by the provinces. We have to draft special agreements to implement Bill No. C-151. The ARDA staff is very small, perhaps 25 or 30 people. We have not increased the staff for about a
Rural Development
year and a half. We are doing our work easily because most of the research that has to be done is done at the provincial level or by special groups. When the projects are submitted to us they are sent to the various departments of government who then accept them or make comments on the proposals that come from the provinces.
There are many other remarks I could make at this point, Mr. Speaker, but I think I have probably given a sufficient explanation, now and when I introduced the bill, to allow hon. members to discuss it in committee. I will be ready to answer specific questions if I can.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has a motion on the order paper that an order of the house do issue for a copy of all reports, briefs or other documents or communications regarding this matter. I wish to say that the matter is now before Mr. Justice Rand who is acting as a commissioner under the Inquiries Act and has this matter under consideration.
Neither the hon. member for Carleton nor anyone else speaking on behalf of this motion has shown that such a brief has any legal significance. The Law Society Act, Revised Statutes of Ontario, 1906, sets out very clearly the powers of that society, particularly in sections 44 to 48. They are to the effect that in any hearing of this kind witnesses shall be subpoenaed and evidence shall be taken. In section 4 the members of the Law Society of Upper Canada are set out, and justices of the Supreme Court of Ontario are not included. Section 3 of the Law Society Act states that judges of the Supreme Court are visitors to the society.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, in my submission the brief made by the Law Society of Upper Canada cannot be held significant as such and can only be dealt with as a recommendation and nothing more. Such a brief could only be based on hearsay, as we understand it. There is no evidence before us that witnesses were properly called or that Mr. Justice Landreville was afforded the opportunity of giving evidence on his own behalf.
I have just been down to the library and looked up the citation of a case regarding a former member of the Law Society of Upper Canada, namely, Samuel Max Mehr. This case is reported in 1955 Supreme Court Reports, at page 344. The appellant was a member of the law society and was disbarred

May 12, 1966
Motions for Papers
by the disciplinary committee for conduct unbecoming a barrister and solicitor. This case was tried by Mr. Justice McRuer. It was appealed to the Supreme Court of Ontario and then to the Supreme Court of Canada. It was clearly pointed out in the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada that the plaintiff must have an opportunity of calling witnesses and defending himself.
Disciplinary powers possessed and exercised by the Law Society of Upper Canada formerly belonged to the courts alone. At the present time the law society has only the powers given to it by the statute I have just mentioned, the Law Society Act. Its powers are very carefully set out in those sections to which I referred.
At the most, any such brief sent to the minister of justice is only a recommendation by the Law Society of Upper Canada. It has no legal status. Its only effect in this house would be to damage the reputation of the judge. The course of action taken in this matter by the Law Society of Upper Canada is most unfortunate. Such a report, I submit, should not have been sent to the Minister of Justice, (Mr. Cardin), and for these reasons I ask hon. members to vote against the motion.

I would suggest that the hon. member knows very well-and this is an opinion very strongly held by members of the profession across the province-that it was most irregular for the benchers, as they did, to assume the responsibility of attacking a particular judge.
The hon. member knows very well from his experience as a bencher that the law society was itself censured by the Supreme Court of Canada approximately a dozen years ago for its conduct of discipline committee proceeding and following a course of conduct which failed to give a fair opportunity to be heard, which failed to accord the principles of natural justice, to another member of the law society. As I say, Mr. Speaker, they were censured in this respect with regard to the procedure of the discipline committee.
What has occurred here is that a group of the benchers-and it is my understanding that it was by no means a unanimous decision

decided to pass judgment upon the conduct of a particular judge and, having incorporated their conclusions upon his conduct in a report, sent that report to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin), at the same time announcing publicly, without making the report public, that they had censured the judge.
I would suggest that this was most extraordinary conduct on the part of the benchers of the Law Society of Upper Canada. We do not know-and perhaps the hon. member can enlighten the house in his five-minute rebuttal -to what extent Mr. Justice Landreville was given notice of the intended course of action

of the benchers. We do not know the extent of the evidence, so-called, which the benchers of the Law Society of Upper Canada received on this particular question before passing judgment. We do not know whether Mr. Justice Landreville was represented at the hearing before the benchers so that the charges against him could be fully examined and arguments could be made on his behalf to the assembled body of the benchers before they arrived at their conclusion.
I suggest that what has occurred here in regard to the conduct of a judge is something that the Supreme Court of Canada said a dozen years ago the law society could not do in respect of an ordinary member of the society. The Supreme Court of Canada said that the law society could not act prejudicially in respect of one of its own members without observing all the requirements of natural justice.
